vignette:
Amir describes his life before the illness with a wistful pride, his hands gesturing as if sculpting a memory in the air. He speaks of the vibrant energy of his salon, a space he built from nothing after arriving from Damascus fifteen years ago. It was his kingdom, filled with the chemical tang of hair dye, the steady snip of his shears, and the easy river of conversation. He was an artist, known for his sharp bobs and masterful color work. He loved the intimacy of it—leaning in to whisper a confidence with a client, the trust they placed in him, the small transformations he created every hour. He was 37, fit, and in command of his world.

That control shattered on a Tuesday morning last year. He was on the treadmill at his gym, pushing for an extra half-mile, when the pressure started. He describes it not as a sharp pain, but as an immense, crushing weight, as if the entire building had settled on his sternum. He remembers the taste of metal in his mouth, the sudden disconnect between his brain telling his legs to run and his body refusing to cooperate. He stumbled off the machine, gasping for air that felt thick and useless. The last thing he clearly recalls is the gym’s fluorescent lights seeming to pulse and dim, and a stranger’s panicked face looming over him, shouting his name.

He woke up in the ICU three days later, a constellation of tubes and wires tethering him to a chorus of beeping machines. Myocardial infarction. The words felt foreign, clinical, a label for something that had felt like a violent, personal assault. The doctors talked about blockages and genetics, but all Amir could feel was the profound betrayal of his own body.

Now, ten months later, his heart is physically healing, but the echo of the trauma reverberates through his life. The salon, once his sanctuary, has become a landscape of triggers. The low hum of a high-powered hairdryer can suddenly sound like the ventilator from the ICU, causing a wave of nausea to roll through him. He’ll be in the middle of a cut, his focus absolute, when he feels a phantom tightness in his chest. His breath catches, his hand trembles, and he has to excuse himself, retreating to the small breakroom to press his fingers against his neck, desperately searching for the steady, rhythmic pulse that will convince him he isn’t dying all over again.

His clients, once a source of energy, now drain him. Their talk of weekend plans and minor work frustrations feels impossibly distant, like broadcasts from another planet. He finds himself staring at his own reflection in the mirror more than the client’s hair, checking the color of his lips, looking for a greyish pallor he remembers seeing in the hospital. He’s developed an irritability that simmers just below the surface, snapping at his assistant over a misplaced bottle of developer, a frustration that is really a mask for his terror.

He no longer goes to the gym. He avoids strenuous activity of any kind, including walking quickly to the corner store. Sleep offers little respite. He often jolts awake in the dark, his heart hammering against his ribs, the memory of suffocating pressure vivid and immediate. He is single and lives alone, and these nights are the worst, filled with a profound sense of isolation and vulnerability. He feels trapped in a body he no longer trusts, a reluctant sentry on perpetual watch for the next, final betrayal. He is physically present, going through the motions of his life, but his mind remains in that hospital bed, forever tethered to the machines that beeped him back to a life he no longer recognizes as his own.
